attacks.claim: The launch sequence commits publicly before the gates pass. Step 3 opens v2 to all, and the blog post says 'Today we're launching', yet the 5xx, p95 and parity gates are evaluated only in step 4. The Deprecation/Sunset headers and the 1,412-recipient email also go out on launch day, and rollback cannot recall them. A failed gate would not stop the launch or the deprecation notice.
attacks.evidence: "3. Publish docs and blog post; open v2 to all. 4. Advance gates: v2 5xx < 0.1%, p95 < 100 ms, parity monitor ≥ 99.9%." and "From launch day, v1 responses carry `Deprecation: @1794787200`"

attacks.claim: One v2 endpoint is said to replace three v1 endpoints, including a route-scoped one and a stop-less /v1/predictions. Only a stop_id parameter is documented. Consumers that filter by route or query without a stop have no documented v2 equivalent, so the replacement claim is unsupported.

`wheelchair_accessible` is a plain boolean with no unknown state, while `crowding` has one and `bike_rack_slots` is nullable. When accessibility data is missing, the API must send true or false. A false value tells a wheelchair user a vehicle is inaccessible when that is not actually known.

Degraded mode has no maximum staleness. After a stall, the last snapshot is served indefinitely with normal-looking ISO arrival times. The only signals are a flag and an age field that apps must choose to read.
attacks.evidence: "responses keep serving the last good snapshot with `feed_age_seconds` set and `meta.degraded: true`; on-call is paged at 120 s."

attacks.claim: The capacity figures do not reconcile. 2.1M requests/day averages about 24 req/s, but the stated v1 peak is 4,100 req/s. The load-test target is derived from the peak. A wrong peak figure would make the sizing basis unreliable.
attacks.evidence: "v1 serves about 2.1M requests/day" and "v1 peak 4,100 req/s → 12,300 req/s on v2"

attacks.claim: Deprecation notice reaches anonymous callers only through response headers. Email goes only to key holders and the top 20 consumers. The 12-month window mitigates this, but nothing says how keyless traffic will be tracked before sunset.
attacks.evidence: "Email to all 1,412 registered key holders on launch day" and "no key required up to 60 requests/min per IP"

attacks.claim: The isolation claim covers only the serving tier, because ingestion is shared. Rollout gates also monitor only v2 metrics, so an ingestion fault would affect v1 and no v1 gate would catch it. Parity testing covers only `arrival_time` on sampled stop/time pairs, not the other replaced endpoints or the new fields.
attacks.evidence: "v2 shares the ingestion pipeline with v1 but runs as a separate deployment and autoscaling group" and "Parity: v2 `arrival_time` vs v1 predictions for 2,000 sampled stop/time pairs"

attacks.claim: The CC BY attribution string names the license but gives no URI. The artifact also states no retention policy for per-IP logs or key-holder contact data.
attacks.evidence: "carry the attribution text \"Contains data from Metro Transit, CC BY 4.0\""

attacks.claim: CORS is open with `*`, but Access-Control-Allow-Headers for X-Api-Key is not specified. Browser apps sending the key may fail preflight. The canary is also described both as a 5% traffic weight and as an allowlist of internal apps and pilot partners, which are different mechanisms.
attacks.evidence: "so browser apps can call it directly." and "Canary: 5% of `/v2/*` traffic for 48 h ... (traffic only from internal apps and the 3 pilot partners who opted in)"
